content: Pruritus, commonly referred to as itch (from the Latin pruritus), is defined as an unpleasant sensation that triggers the desire or reflex to scratch. Itch shares many similarities with pain, as both are unpleasant sensory experiences. However, their behavioral response patterns differ significantly. Pain typically induces a reflex withdrawal to protect the body, while itch leads to a scratching reflex aimed at alleviating the sensation. Both itch and pain originate in the skin and are transmitted centrally via distinct systems, despite utilizing the same peripheral nerve bundles and spinothalamic tract. Historically, itch and pain were not considered independent sensations until recent findings demonstrated that, while they share some features, they exhibit notable differences. The physiological mechanisms underlying itch remain poorly understood, largely due to the lack of reliable animal models for studying itch. While pruritic stimuli often elicit similar reactions to noxious stimuli in experimental animals, humans can distinguish between the two sensations. Consequently, most of the current understanding of pruritic processing comes from human studies. Mechanisms of Itch Itch can originate from the peripheral nervous system (dermal or neuropathic) or the central nervous system (neuropathic, neurogenic, or psychogenic). Dermal/Pruritocaptive Itch Itch originating in the skin is classified as pruritocaptive and can be triggered by various stimuli, including mechanical, chemical, thermal, and electrical stimulation. The primary afferent neurons responsible for histamine-induced itch are unmyelinated C-fibers. In human C-fiber nociceptors, two major classes exist: mechano-responsive nociceptors, which primarily respond to pain, and mechano-insensitive nociceptors, which predominantly respond to histamine-induced itch. However, this does not explain mechanically induced itch or itch that occurs without a histamine-mediated flare reaction. This suggests the existence of different classes of pruritocaptive nerve fibers, though this remains unclear in current research. Studies have shown that itch receptors are located only in the top two layers of the skin: the epidermis and the epidermal-dermal transition layer. Shelley and Arthur confirmed this by injecting individual itch powder spicules (from Mucuna pruriens) and found maximal sensitivity at the basal cell layer, the innermost layer of the epidermis. Surgical removal of these skin layers eliminates the ability to perceive itch. Itch is never felt in muscles, joints, or internal organs, indicating that deep tissues lack itch-signaling apparatuses. Sensitivity to pruritic stimuli is uneven across the skin, with a random spot distribution similar to that of pain. Substances that elicit itch when injected intradermally cause only pain when injected subcutaneously. Itch can be abolished in skin areas treated with the nociceptor excitotoxin capsaicin but remains unchanged in areas rendered touch-insensitive by pretreatment with saponins, an anti-inflammatory agent. Experimentally induced itch can still be perceived under a complete A-fiber conduction block, though it is significantly diminished. Overall, itch sensation is mediated by A-delta and C nociceptors located in the uppermost skin layers. Neuropathic Itch Neuropathic itch can arise at any point along the afferent pathway due to damage to the nervous system. This includes diseases or disorders affecting the central or peripheral nervous systems. Examples of neuropathic itch include nostalgia paresthetica, brachioradial pruritus, brain tumors, multiple sclerosis, peripheral neuropathy, and nerve irritation. Neurogenic Itch Neurogenic itch is centrally induced without neural damage and is often associated with increased levels of endogenous opioids or synthetic opioids. Psychogenic Itch Psychogenic itch is linked to psychiatric disorders, such as delusions of parasitosis or obsessive-compulsive disorders, including neurotic scratching. Interactions Between Itch and Pain Pain Inhibits Itch The sensation of itch can be reduced by various painful stimuli. Numerous studies have demonstrated that itch can be inhibited by noxious heat, physical rubbing or scratching, noxious chemicals, and electric shocks. Any stimulus that causes pain can suppress itching. This inhibition likely operates through central mechanisms rather than peripheral ones. For example, noxious heat and scratching have been shown to inhibit histamine-induced itch and even reduce skin blood flow. Painful electrical stimulation can suppress histamine-induced itch for several hours, even at a distance of up to 10 cm from the stimulated site, suggesting a central mode of action. A novel method called cutaneous field stimulation (CFS) has been developed to relieve itch without damaging the skin. CFS involves a flexible rubber plate with needle-like electrodes that electrically stimulate nerve fibers in the skin's surface. This method activates nociceptive C-fibers and creates a long-lasting inhibitory effect on itch. Sensations Associated with Scratching Pain and itch elicit distinct behavioral responses. Pain triggers a withdrawal reflex to protect the body, while itch induces a scratching reflex that draws attention to the affected skin site. Scratching has traditionally been viewed as a way to relieve itch by reducing the sensation. However, scratching can also have hedonic aspects, as noxious scratching is often perceived as highly pleasurable. This can be problematic for chronic itch patients, such as those with atopic dermatitis, who may scratch until the sensation becomes neither pleasant nor painful, rather than when the itch subsides. Contagious Itch Contagious itch is a common phenomenon where discussing or observing itch can induce the desire to scratch. Itch is likely more than a localized phenomenon, as visual stimuli alone can trigger itching and scratching. This may involve a human mirror neuron system, similar to the mechanism behind contagious yawning. Causes of Itch Common causes of itch include xerosis, eczema, psoriasis, sunburn, athlete's foot, insect bites, urushiol exposure, Hodgkin's disease, jaundice, polycythemia, scabies, lice, thyroid disorders, shaving, diabetes mellitus, dandruff, iron deficiency anemia, parasitic infections, allergies, and certain medications (e.g., morphine, terbinafine, niacin, simvastatin). Diagnosis and Treatment A thorough medical history, including family, exposure, and sexual history, is essential for diagnosing the underlying cause of itch. Physical examination and laboratory tests, such as CBC, liver function tests, renal function tests, thyroid function tests, and tests for HIV, hepatitis, and parasites, can help identify contributing factors. Treatment options include over-the-counter and prescription anti-itch medications, as well as non-chemical remedies like cooling, warming, and soft stimulation. Maintaining adequate skin moisture and using topical emollients are crucial for managing dry skin. However, scratching can sometimes exacerbate itching and cause further skin damage, perpetuating the itch-scratch-itch cycle.
